From 1 January 2026 the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism entered its definitive phase, after a transitional period in which importers merely reported the emissions embedded in their goods. Steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, electricity and hydrogen are covered first; importers will in time have to buy certificates priced by reference to the Union’s carbon market, less any carbon price already paid in the country of origin. India, whose exports of steel and aluminium to the Union are significant, has called such measures unilateral trade barriers dressed as climate policy, even as its negotiators have pursued a trade agreement with Brussels and prepared an updated climate pledge, expected by the end of the year. The collision of these tracks makes the mechanism a useful case study in a question that will recur: when does a carbon charge at the border protect the climate, and when does it merely protect producers?

The case for a border adjustment begins with leakage. If one jurisdiction prices carbon and its trading partners do not, production can migrate to the unpriced jurisdiction, so that emissions fall at home and rise abroad, and domestic industry is penalised for its virtue. A levy on the embedded carbon of imports levels the field and removes the incentive to relocate. It also changes the politics: producers who would otherwise lobby against a higher domestic carbon price lose their strongest argument, and the border measure can therefore make a stricter domestic price sustainable. Without it, a government might fear that a high carbon price would simply export the factories along with the emissions.

Exporting countries raise three objections. The first concerns fairness. The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, written into the climate regime, holds that countries which industrialised first and emitted most should bear the heavier burden of cutting emissions. A charge levied on goods from poorer economies, at a rate set by a richer economy’s carbon market, applies one standard to unequal circumstances. Defenders respond that the charge falls on the product and not on the country, and treats a tonne of steel identically whoever made it. The response is formally correct, but it hardly meets the point, since the capacity to decarbonise steel is itself unequally distributed.

The second objection concerns where the money goes. Because importers may deduct carbon prices paid at home, an exporter that taxes its own producers keeps the revenue, while one that does not effectively sends the equivalent to Brussels. The arithmetic therefore rewards the adoption of domestic carbon pricing, which is one reason several developing countries, India among them, have been building carbon markets of their own. The mechanism thus works partly as an inducement. Whether an inducement imposed by a large buyer is persuasion or pressure depends on whether the exporter would have chosen the same policy unprompted, which is precisely what cannot be observed.

The third objection is administrative. To claim a deduction, or to avoid the default values that importers use when data are missing, exporters must measure the emissions embedded in each shipment to the importer’s standard and have them verified. For large firms this is a cost; for small and medium exporters it is a largely fixed cost that does not shrink with volume, and so it falls hardest on those least able to bear it. Default values are often set conservatively, so the exporters least able to measure may end up paying the most. A measure designed to tax carbon may thus, in part, tax paperwork.

Who bears the charge is also less obvious than the rhetoric implies. If the exporter has few alternative buyers, the charge is absorbed in lower prices received; if the importer has few alternative suppliers, it is passed on to buyers within the Union. The shares depend on the responsiveness of supply and demand, not on the name printed on the certificate. Where the Union takes a large part of a country’s output of a particular good, the exporter is likely to bear much of the charge; where the good is widely traded, the burden spreads and may fall largely on European consumers.

The exporting side’s strongest reply is not that carbon should go unpriced but that the instrument is blunt. It covers a handful of sectors, taxes the emissions of a foreign product at the border while leaving untouched much of the carbon embedded in the importer’s own consumption, and may conflict with trade rules that forbid discrimination between like products unless justified by a recognised exception. Defenders cite the environmental exception in those rules; critics answer that an exception must not become a disguise for protection, and that the test is whether the measure would survive if the importing industry lost its stake in it.

There is, finally, a dynamic question. A charge that tracks the Union’s carbon price will rise and fall with it, so an exporter deciding whether to invest in lower-emission steelmaking must forecast a price set in another jurisdiction by decisions it cannot influence. Investments in cleaner plant last decades, while the charge may be revised within a few years. Uncertainty of this kind can delay precisely the investment that the mechanism is meant to encourage, and it is one reason exporters have asked for predictable rules and, where possible, a say in how they are revised.

What the case shows is that the same measure can be at once a genuine instrument of climate policy and an instrument of industrial policy, and that the two descriptions are not rival hypotheses to be decided between but overlapping facts. The useful questions are about design: whether the charge is calibrated to the carbon actually embedded rather than to a convenient proxy, whether revenue is returned to the countries that pay it, whether help with measurement is offered to those who must comply, and whether the measure is accompanied by finance for decarbonisation abroad. A measure that answers these questions looks like climate policy; one that does not looks like tariff protection with a green label, whatever its authors intend.
questions.question: The author’s reply to the defenders’ claim that the charge falls on the product and not on the country implies that
options: A) the charge is unlawful, since a levy that is applied to goods rather than to countries cannot be reconciled with the climate regime
B) treating every product alike can still yield unequal burdens when the capacity to decarbonise is unequal
C) richer countries should be exempt from the charge, because their steelmakers have already paid for the carbon that they emit
D) the defenders have misunderstood the mechanism, which in fact treats a tonne of steel differently according to who has made it
questions.explanation: Explanation: Para 3: the response is ‘formally correct’ but misses the point because the capacity to decarbonise is unequally distributed. Identical treatment is therefore compatible with unequal burden. The author does not call the charge unlawful, propose exemptions, or deny that products are treated alike.

questions.question: The claim that the deduction for carbon prices paid at home works as an “inducement” presupposes that
options: A) every developing country that has built a carbon market did so only after being warned that its exports would be charged at the border
B) the importing authority sets the level of the deduction so as to ensure that exporters never pay anything at all to the importing authority
C) exporters that tax their own producers are able to pass the whole of the domestic tax on to buyers in the importing country concerned
D) exporters are likelier to adopt carbon pricing if it lets them keep revenue that would otherwise be paid abroad
questions.explanation: Explanation: Para 4: ‘the arithmetic rewards’ domestic pricing. The inducement works only if exporters respond to the prospect of keeping revenue; negate this and the deduction induces nothing. The other options are absolutes or claims the passage never makes (it says the exporter’s counterfactual choice ‘cannot be observed’).

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that the administrative burden “falls hardest on those least able to bear it”?
options: A) Small exporters mostly sell through large intermediaries that carry the measurement burden.
B) Default values used by importers when data are missing have been revised upwards for all exporters in each of the sectors covered so far.
C) Large firms have reported that the cost of verification is the main reason they have hesitated to expand exports to the Union as planned.
D) Several exporting countries have asked the importing authority to accept their own national standards of measurement in place of its own.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Para 5 rests on small exporters facing a fixed cost themselves. If intermediaries carry that cost, the burden no longer falls on them. The other options concern default values, large firms or standards, not who bears the cost.

questions.question: It follows from the paragraph on who bears the charge that
options: A) the party named on the certificate bears the charge in every market, since legal liability fixes where the cost finally falls
B) European consumers bear the whole of the charge on any good that the Union imports, whatever the alternatives open to its suppliers
C) an exporter with few alternative buyers is likely to bear more of the charge than one with many
D) the charge can have no effect on prices received by exporters, because importers add it to the price that they charge their customers
questions.explanation: Explanation: Para 5 (incidence): shares depend on the responsiveness of supply and demand, not on the name on the certificate; with few alternative buyers the charge is absorbed in lower prices received. C) it serves its speakers as a marker of belonging and is bound up with their confidence as a community

questions.explanation: Explanation: Paras 2–3 give the scientific and identity arguments. Para 3 says a dominant language, not a small one, opens ‘schools, markets and jobs’, so better economic opportunity is the opposite of what the passage says.

questions.passage:
Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that about forty per cent are endangered, and that a language falls silent, on average, every few weeks. These figures are contested, since there is no census of speakers for most small languages and the definition of “endangered” varies, but the direction of the trend is not disputed. The United Nations has declared a decade of Indigenous languages, and governments from Wales to New Zealand fund schools and broadcasts in minority tongues. Behind this activity lies an argument that deserves examination, because it is not obvious. Why should the loss of a language matter, and to whom?

The first answer is scientific. Each language is a record of how a group of people has categorised its world, and its loss destroys information that cannot be recovered. Languages carry vocabularies for local plants, seasons and technologies; they preserve oral histories; and they provide linguists with the variation needed to discover what is universal in human language and what is accidental. A theory of grammar based on a dozen major languages would be a theory of a very unrepresentative sample. This argument is strong but limited. It supports documentation, in the form of recordings, dictionaries and grammars, more clearly than it supports survival, since a language that has been fully recorded has, for the scientist’s purposes, been saved even if no child speaks it.

The second answer is about identity and dignity. A language is for its speakers not merely a tool but a marker of belonging, and its decline often accompanies a decline in the community’s confidence. Here the argument concerns the speakers rather than the scientists, and it is therefore more powerful, but also harder to apply: it requires that the speakers themselves wish to keep the language. The history of language shift shows that they often do not. Parents who stop speaking their language to their children are rarely acting out of ignorance. They are responding to an economy in which a dominant language opens schools, markets and jobs, and a small language does not.

That response exposes the economic logic of language death. A language is a network good: its value to each speaker rises with the number of others who speak it, so that a language with many speakers attracts still more, and one with few loses them, in a self-reinforcing process. Once a threshold is crossed, each family’s rational choice to switch contributes to making switching more rational for the next. Nobody intends the result, and nobody, individually, can reverse it. This has the structure of a coordination problem, in which the outcome that is best for the group, the survival of the language, may require everyone to act against immediate interest. It is one reason why exhortation alone fails, and why successful revivals have usually involved institutions, such as schools and public employment, that change the payoff of speaking the language.

Critics of preservation put the opposing view. If people choose to shift, they argue, it is paternalistic for outsiders to stand in the way; a language is not a museum piece, and to oblige a community to maintain it for the sake of the world’s diversity is to ask the poor to subsidise the curiosity of the comfortable. There is force in this, and a policy that treats speakers as custodians instead of as people with ambitions deserves the criticism. But the argument assumes that the choice is free. Where a language was suppressed in schools, as with many Indigenous languages in North America and Australia, or stigmatised in the labour market, the shift was not simply a preference but a response to penalties imposed by others. Whether to honour such a choice depends on the conditions under which it was made, and in many cases those conditions were not neutral.

Technology complicates the picture in both directions. Digital media and machine translation have lowered the cost of publishing in a small language, and some communities use messaging applications and online dictionaries to keep their languages in daily use among the young. Yet the same networks strengthen the pull of the dominant languages, in which most content, software and commerce are produced. Whether a language benefits depends on whether its speakers can find in it the services they need, which is again a question of how many others are present to provide them, and so of the network logic described above. A language that platforms do not support may be preserved online as a curiosity without ever becoming usable in daily life.

The record of revival is mixed. Hebrew, restored from largely liturgical use to a daily language, is an exceptional case, sustained by a state, by immigration and by a pressing need for a common tongue. Welsh has recovered some ground through schooling and broadcasting, though the use of the language in the home has risen less than the number who have learned it at school. Irish shows the gap between official status and daily use: it is a national and official language taught to every child, and yet is used daily by only a small fraction of the population. The lesson is that teaching a language in school produces speakers but not necessarily a speech community, and a language needs the second in order to survive.

The sensible conclusion is that the case for preserving languages is a cluster of arguments of different strength, addressed to different audiences. For scientists, documentation may be enough; for speakers, what matters is the freedom to use the language without penalty and the realistic possibility of passing it on; for outsiders, the question is what they owe to communities whose languages are declining under pressures that outsiders helped to create. Treating these as one argument invites the objection that is easiest to make, that preservation is sentimental. Taken separately, each is sturdier.
questions.question: The author’s remark that, taken separately, each argument is “sturdier” implies that
options: A) the arguments for preservation are all of equal strength, so that it does not matter which of them is used to defend it
B) preservation is in fact sentimental, and none of the arguments that have been advanced can survive a serious test of them
C) combining arguments aimed at different audiences exposes the whole case to the weakest of them
D) the three audiences, scientists, speakers and outsiders, have interests that are identical and so can be addressed together
questions.explanation: Explanation: Final para: treating the arguments as one invites the easiest objection (that preservation is sentimental), so a combined case is only as strong as its weakest part. The passage says the arguments differ in strength and audience.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Defaults work because most people stick with whatever option requires no action.
2. In countries where citizens must actively opt in to organ donation, consent rates are low.
3. Where donation is the default and people must opt out, rates are far higher.
4. The difference cannot be explained by differences in values, which are broadly similar.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 gives the opt-in case, 3 the opt-out contrast, 4 rules out values as the cause, and 1 (‘Defaults work because…’) supplies the explanation.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Within a generation, the language survives only among the old.
2. Languages rarely vanish because they are forbidden; more often parents simply stop passing them on.
3. They do so because a dominant language seems to offer their children better prospects.
4. Within two, it is gone, and with it a vocabulary that no other tongue records.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 states the general claim, 3 (‘They do so’) gives the reason, 1 (‘Within a generation’) the first stage, and 4 (‘Within two’) the end.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. The strategy works, however, only if the threat is believed.
2. A firm that threatens to cut prices whenever a rival enters the market hopes to deter entry.
3. A threat that would harm the firm itself if carried out is therefore not credible.
4. Economists call such threats empty and expect rivals to ignore them.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 introduces the threat, 1 (‘however’) the condition, 3 (‘therefore’) the implication, and 4 (‘such threats’) the label and consequence.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. The remedy, they argue, is to measure performance over several years.
2. Critics say that annual reviews reward managers for short-term gains that later prove illusory.
3. A manager can lift this year’s profit by cutting maintenance, whose cost appears only afterwards.
4. Longer horizons make such cuts harder to hide.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 states the criticism, 3 gives the illustration, 1 (‘The remedy’) the proposed fix, and 4 (‘such cuts’) the reason it works.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Over time, however, the bridge’s cables began to corrode.
2. The engineers had chosen a steel they believed would resist the salt air.
3. Inspections therefore became more frequent, and costs rose.
4. For the first decade it performed without any trouble.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 gives the design choice, 4 the good early record, 1 (‘Over time, however’) the change, and 3 (‘therefore’) the consequence.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Adding a new road to a network can lengthen everyone’s journey. When each driver chooses the fastest route, the new link attracts so many that congestion rises elsewhere, and the resulting equilibrium is slower than before, even though no driver has acted irrationally. The paradox shows that individually sensible choices need not add up to the best collective outcome, and that more capacity does not guarantee faster travel.'
options: A) Selfish route choices mean extra capacity can slow everyone, so individual rationality may yield worse collective outcomes.
B) New roads always increase journey times, since drivers are irrational and cannot be relied upon to pick the fastest route available to them.
C) Congestion can be removed only by building new links, because drivers who choose their own routes will always make the network slower for others.
D) The paradox shows that planners should never add capacity to a network, because the effect of new roads on journey times is unpredictable.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph states Braess’s paradox: rational choices can produce a worse collective result. The distractors say ‘always’, claim drivers are irrational, or draw policy conclusions the paragraph does not.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Studies at the Hawthorne plant once suggested that workers improved simply because they knew they were being observed. Later re-analyses found the original data thinner than reported and the effect smaller, though the broader lesson, that being studied can change behaviour, has survived in experimental design, where researchers use control groups and blinding to separate the effect of a treatment from the effect of attention.'
options: A) The Hawthorne studies proved conclusively that workers always work harder when watched, and modern experiments are designed around that finding.
B) Though the Hawthorne evidence was weaker than claimed, the idea that observation alters behaviour endures and justifies controls and blinding.
C) The Hawthorne studies were fraudulent, so the idea that being observed changes behaviour has been dropped from the design of experiments.
D) Control groups and blinding were invented by the Hawthorne researchers, who were the first to see that attention could affect their results.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph says the original evidence was thinner than reported but the lesson survives in controls and blinding. The distractors overstate, call the studies fraudulent, or invent an origin for controls.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Gresham’s law says that bad money drives out good: where two coins of equal face value but different metal content circulate, people hoard the one with more precious metal and spend the debased one. The law holds when the exchange rate between the coins is fixed by decree; where the market can price the coins by their content, the better coin can still circulate at a premium.'
options: A) Bad money always drives out good, because people everywhere prefer to spend debased coins and to hoard those with more precious metal.
B) Governments should never fix the exchange rate between coins, since a market price is the only means of preventing the debasement of money.
C) Bad money drives out good only where official values ignore content; free pricing can let good coins circulate.
D) Good coins circulate at a premium in every economy, which proves that Gresham’s law has never held in any period of monetary history.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The law is conditional on fixed values; with market pricing the good coin can circulate at a premium. The distractors drop the condition or draw sweeping policy and historical claims.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone. A student who spends an evening at a ten-pound concert has therefore paid more than ten pounds if ________.'
options: A) the time could have been put to a valuable alternative use
B) the concert was so enjoyable that she would have been willing to pay a far higher price to attend it on the same evening
C) the ticket was bought at a discount, because the price that she paid was then lower than the usual price of the ticket
D) she would not have gone to the concert had she not been given the ticket, because the evening would have been wasted
questions.explanation: Explanation: Opportunity cost adds the value of the next best use of time to the money price. The distractors discuss willingness to pay, discounts or the gift of a ticket, none of which adds a forgone alternative.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Correlation does not imply causation. Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together in summer, yet neither causes the other; both are driven by ________.'
options: A) the habit of eating ice cream before swimming, which leads to cramps and so makes drowning more likely at crowded beaches
B) a common cause, the warmth of the season
C) the fact that people who drown tend to have bought ice cream earlier, which shows that the sales have caused the drownings
D) the chance coincidence of two unrelated series of data, which can never be explained by any factor that lies behind them
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph says neither causes the other, so the link is a third factor (hot weather). The distractors reintroduce a causal link or deny any common factor.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'PELLUCID':
options: A) Lucid
B) Opaque
C) Bewildering
D) Convoluted
questions.explanation: Explanation: Pellucid means translucently clear or easily understood; ‘lucid’ is closest. The others suggest obscurity.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'TACITURN':
options: A) Uncommunicative
B) Reserved
C) Talkative
D) Silent
questions.explanation: Explanation: Taciturn means habitually silent; ‘talkative’ is the antonym. The others are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'TENACIOUS':
options: A) Irresolute
B) Dogged
C) Languid
D) Compliant
questions.explanation: Explanation: Tenacious means holding firmly to a purpose; ‘dogged’ is closest. The others suggest weakness or yielding.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'BENEVOLENT':
options: A) Philanthropic
B) Altruistic
C) Charitable
D) Malign
questions.explanation: Explanation: Benevolent means well-meaning and kindly; ‘malign’ (harmful in intent) is the opposite.

questions.question:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:
'The minister’s reply was deliberately ________, offering neither a promise nor a refusal.'
options: A) unequivocal
B) unambiguous
C) evasive
D) forthright
questions.explanation: Explanation: A reply that neither promises nor refuses is ‘evasive’. The others mean direct and clear.

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills the blanks:
'The reviews were so ________ that audiences, expecting a masterpiece, felt ________ when they saw the film.'
options: A) glowing; let down
B) scathing; unsurprised
C) lukewarm; enthusiastic
D) indifferent; overjoyed
questions.explanation: Explanation: Very favourable reviews raise expectations, so a weaker film leaves viewers ‘let down’. In the other pairs the second word does not follow logically from the first.

questions.question:
Choose the correct idiom meaning:
'To burn the midnight oil' means to:
options: A) waste resources carelessly on lamps and fuel
B) work late into the night
C) start a quarrel late at night in the family home
D) cook a meal after everyone else has gone to sleep
questions.explanation: Explanation: The idiom comes from working by lamplight after dark.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which 'LITERALLY' is used in its standard sense:
options: A) The play was so funny that I literally died laughing in my seat.
B) She was literally over the moon when she heard her result.
C) The map literally places the village in the wrong valley.
D) The traffic was literally a nightmare that went on for years.
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Literally’ in its standard sense means in actual fact. The others use it as an intensifier for figurative statements.

questions.question: Select the option that best gives the meaning of 'OBFUSCATE':
options: A) bring a difficult matter to a speedy and satisfactory end
B) argue forcefully against a proposal that others have made
C) repeat the same point over and over again at great length
D) make something unclear or hard to understand
questions.explanation: Explanation: To obfuscate is to make obscure or confusing.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'Each of the candidates ________ interviewed separately.'
options: A) were
B) was
C) are
D) have been
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Each’ takes a singular verb: ‘was interviewed’.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'She is taller (A) / than any (B) / girl in (C) / her class (D).'
options: A) She is taller
B) than any
C) girl in
D) her class
questions.explanation: Explanation: A comparison within a group needs ‘any other’: ‘taller than any other girl in her class’.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) Hardly had he left when it started to rain.
B) Scarcely had he left than it started raining on the road home.
C) He denied to have taken the money from the safe in the office.
D) She prefers tea than coffee in the morning before she goes to work.
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Hardly… when’ is correct. The others misuse ‘than’, the infinitive after ‘denied’ (needs ‘having taken’) and ‘prefers… than’ (needs ‘to’).

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'He insisted that she ________ present at the meeting.'
options: A) is
B) was
C) be
D) would be
questions.explanation: Explanation: After ‘insist that’ the subjunctive (‘be’) is used.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'The professor, along with his students, ________ attending the conference.'
options: A) are
B) is
C) were
D) have been
questions.explanation: Explanation: The subject is ‘professor’; ‘along with his students’ is parenthetical, so the verb is singular.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'Having finished (A) / the exam, the bell (B) / rang and the students (C) / left the hall (D).'
options: A) the exam, the bell
B) Having finished
C) rang and the students
D) left the hall
questions.explanation: Explanation: Dangling modifier: ‘Having finished the exam’ must modify the students, not the bell.

questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
'She is allergic ________ penicillin.'
options: A) with
B) from
C) against
D) to
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Allergic’ takes ‘to’.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) I have been living in this city since the year 2019 began.
B) He is senior than me by two years.
C) She prefers walking to driving whenever the distance is short.
D) The children were made to apologise to their teacher at once.
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Senior’ takes ‘to’, not ‘than’: ‘senior to me’.
